pages.text: Rakan had expected his summer in Abha to be a complete waste of time. Instead of hanging out with his friends in Riyadh, he had been sent to help his uncle Saeed in a tiny bookshop on a steep, foggy street. The shop smelled of dust and cardamom, and on most mornings hardly anyone came in. "Patience," his uncle kept saying, as he arranged the same shelves for the third time. "Books choose their readers slowly."

There was one customer, however, who came every Thursday without fail. He was an elderly man with a carefully trimmed white beard and a walking stick, and he always went straight to the poetry section. He would take down the same faded green book, sit in the corner chair, and stay there for nearly an hour. Then he would return it to the shelf, thank them politely, and leave without buying a thing. "He's been doing that for months," Rakan complained. "Why don't you just tell him it's not a library?"

Uncle Saeed looked at him over his glasses. "Some things are worth more than the price on the cover," he replied, but he refused to explain. The following Thursday, Rakan decided to pay closer attention. He noticed that the old man held the book unusually close to his face and that his finger moved slowly beneath each line. Sometimes he stopped on a page for so long that Rakan wondered whether he had fallen asleep.

It wasn't until the fourth week that it finally dawned on Rakan what was happening. As the man stood up, he bumped into a table and almost knocked over a pile of dictionaries. Rakan rushed over to help, and the man laughed with embarrassment. "Forgive me, my son," he said. "My eyes are not what they used to be, and the doctor says that soon I won't be able to read at all."

That evening, Rakan couldn't stop thinking about the green book. With his uncle's permission, he took it home and discovered that it was a collection of old poems about the mountains, the rain and the people of the south. Some of the words were difficult, but gradually he began to understand why someone might read them again and again. Then an idea struck him out of the blue. He borrowed his cousin's microphone, shut himself in his room, and started to record himself reading the poems aloud.

It was far harder than he had imagined. His voice cracked, the neighbour's goats kept interrupting, and he had to start some poems over a dozen times. By Wednesday night, though, he had recorded every single page. His uncle listened to a few minutes in silence, then put a hand on his shoulder. "You have gone the extra mile, Rakan," he said quietly, "and nobody even had to ask you."

On Thursday, the old man arrived as usual, but this time the green book was waiting for him on the counter, wrapped in brown paper with a small speaker beside it. Rakan explained, a little nervously, what he had done. For a long moment the man said nothing, and Rakan worried that he might have offended him. Then the man pressed play, and as Rakan's voice filled the shop, his eyes grew wet. "You have given me back something I thought I had lost forever," he whispered.

When Rakan refused to accept any money, the old man smiled and opened the book to its first page. "Do you know why I come here to read this particular book?" he asked. He pointed to a name printed beneath the title: Abdullah Al-Ghamdi. "Forty years ago, I wrote these poems," he said, "and your grandfather was the only bookseller brave enough to sell them." Rakan stared at him, completely lost for words.

Uncle Saeed had known all along, of course. For the rest of the summer, Abdullah came every Thursday, and Rakan read new poems to him while the old man shared stories about Abha in the old days. When it was finally time to return to Riyadh, Rakan realised he no longer considered the summer a waste. He had learned that kindness is rarely about grand gestures; more often, it begins with simply noticing someone. In his bag, carefully wrapped, was a faded green book of his own, signed by its author.

pages.text: For weeks, Layla had been begging her grandfather to take her kayaking in the mangroves of the Farasan Islands. Jaddi Saleh had spent thirty years in the coast guard, and he knew those twisting green channels better than anyone in the family. "The mangroves are beautiful, but they can be tricky," he warned her the night before. "Don't bite off more than you can chew." Layla, who was fourteen and felt perfectly capable of anything, just smiled and promised to listen.

They set off early the next afternoon, their double kayak sliding smoothly across the calm, turquoise water. As they paddled, Jaddi shared the lessons he had learned at sea. "The sea talks, if you are patient enough to listen," he said. "When the tide is going out, the water always flows towards the open sea, so it can show you the way home." Layla nodded politely, although she was more interested in the pink flamingos standing in the shallows.

Deep among the mangroves, Layla took dozens of photos of herons and crabs, and they completely lost track of time. When she finally looked up, she noticed that the bright sky had turned a strange, milky white. Within minutes, a thick fog had rolled in from the sea, swallowing the trees around them. "Stay calm," Jaddi said quietly, but she could hear the worry hidden in his voice. Every channel now looked exactly the same.

Trying to find a way out, they got stuck on a sandbank, and Jaddi climbed out to push the kayak free. Suddenly, his foot slipped on a hidden root, and he fell with a sharp cry of pain. By the time Layla had helped him back into his seat, his ankle was already swelling badly. She pulled out her phone to call her uncle, but there was no signal at all. For the first time that day, Layla felt genuinely afraid.

"You'll have to paddle us back, my dear," Jaddi said, his face pale. Layla took a deep breath and told herself to keep a cool head. She tried to remember everything he had told her earlier, words she had barely been paying attention to. Then she noticed a few dry leaves floating on the surface, drifting slowly but steadily in one direction. "The tide is going out," she whispered. "The water is showing us the way."

Layla followed the floating leaves, paddling harder than she had ever paddled before. However, the channel soon split into three narrow paths, and the current seemed to fade away completely. She chose the widest one, only to find that it led to a dead end blocked by fallen branches. Meanwhile, the water level was dropping fast, and if it fell much further, the kayak would be trapped in the mud until morning. Her arms ached, and the light was beginning to disappear.

Just as she was about to give up, a faint sound drifted through the fog. It was the Maghrib call to prayer, rising from the mosque in the fishing village near the harbour. Layla's heart leapt, because she knew the mosque stood right beside the beach where they had started. Turning the kayak until the sound was directly ahead of her, she chose the channel where the current felt strongest. Sound and water were pointing the same way at last.

Ten minutes later, the mangroves suddenly opened up, and the kayak glided out into wide, open water. Through the thinning fog, Layla spotted the swinging beam of a torch on a small fishing boat. "Over here!" she shouted, waving her paddle wildly above her head. It was her uncle Khalid, who had come looking for them when they hadn't returned. They had arrived in the nick of time, because the channel behind them was already turning to mud.

That evening, with his ankle wrapped in a bandage, Jaddi asked Layla how she had found the right path. When she mentioned the call to prayer, he laughed and shook his head in amazement. "I never taught you that trick," he admitted. "You worked it out all by yourself, which makes it far more valuable than anything I could have taught you." The next day, Layla drew a careful map of the mangroves, and beside the hidden channel that had saved them, Jaddi proudly wrote two words: Layla's Way.

pages.text: The ferry from Jazan cut through water so blue that Faisal could hardly believe it was real. He had come to the Farasan Islands to spend two weeks with his aunt Huda, a marine biologist who studied hawksbill turtles. "Don't expect a holiday," she warned him with a smile as she picked him up at the port. "We work at night, we sleep in the afternoon, and we never, ever leave rubbish on the sand." Faisal, who was fifteen and had never stayed up past midnight on purpose, nodded as if this were perfectly normal.

On his first night, they walked along a quiet beach with red torches, which turtles find less disturbing than white light. Aunt Huda knelt beside a small circle of sticks pushed into the sand. "About a hundred eggs are buried here," she whispered. "They were laid nearly two months ago, so they could hatch any night now." She explained that newborn turtles find the sea by crawling towards the brightest horizon, which is usually moonlight shining on the water. "For millions of years, that rule has worked perfectly," she added, "but people keep changing the rules."

The next morning, Faisal noticed something he had missed in the dark. Just behind the dunes, a brand-new café was almost finished, and workers were hanging long strings of bright white bulbs along its roof. A large sign announced the grand opening for Thursday evening. Faisal's stomach dropped, because Thursday was only two days away. "If those lights are switched on," he said slowly, "the baby turtles will think the café is the sea."

Aunt Huda immediately phoned the environmental office in Jazan, but the officer she needed was away until the following week. She wrote an official report, sent photos and left three messages, yet nobody replied. "These things take time," she sighed, rubbing her tired eyes. "Unfortunately, turtles don't wait for paperwork." Faisal paced up and down the small kitchen, feeling that they were running out of time.

That afternoon, without telling anyone, Faisal walked over to the café and asked to speak to the owner. Abu Saleh was a busy man with a phone in each hand, and at first he barely looked up. "Turtles?" he said, raising his eyebrows. "Young man, I've spent my savings on this place, and I need people to see it from the road." Faisal tried to explain about the nest and the moonlight, but the owner had already turned away to shout instructions at an electrician. Faisal left feeling foolish, wishing he had chosen his words more carefully.

On Wednesday night, a day earlier than anyone had expected, the sand inside the circle of sticks began to move. First one tiny flipper appeared, then a head, then dozens of small dark shapes pushed their way to the surface. At that exact moment, the café lights flashed on for a final test, and the whole beach glowed as if it were midday. To Faisal's horror, the hatchlings hesitated for a second and then turned away from the waves. One by one, they began crawling up the beach towards the dunes and the busy road beyond.

Faisal didn't stop to think; he simply ran. He burst into the café, where Abu Saleh was checking the decorations with his teenage son, Saleh. "Please, come and look, just for one minute!" Faisal begged, completely out of breath. Perhaps it was the panic in his voice, but the owner followed him outside. When he saw the trail of tiny turtles heading straight for the car park, his face changed completely, and he shouted to his son, "Switch everything off, now!"

Within seconds, the beach fell into darkness, and the silver line of moonlight on the sea became the brightest thing in sight again. Slowly, as if waking from a confusing dream, the hatchlings turned around. Aunt Huda, Faisal, Saleh and even Abu Saleh knelt on the sand, gently guiding the slowest ones with their red torches. For almost an hour, nobody said a word as the little turtles reached the wet sand and were carried away by the waves. "I had no idea," Abu Saleh finally murmured, shaking his head.

The café opened on Thursday after all, but it looked rather different from the plans. Abu Saleh had replaced the white bulbs with soft, low amber lights that turtles cannot easily see, and he had added a board explaining how visitors could protect the nests. A month later, back home in Riyadh, Faisal received a photo from Saleh showing the café's new name above the door: Hatchling Café. Underneath, Abu Saleh had written, "Thank you for not giving up on an old, stubborn man." Faisal smiled and realised that sometimes the bravest thing you can do is knock on a door twice.

pages.text: Faris Al-Harbi had always believed that the sky above AlUla was the clearest in the world. On summer nights, when the heat finally faded from the sandstone cliffs, he would climb onto the roof with his grandfather and watch satellites crossing the stars like slow, silent sparks. His grandfather, a retired engineer, had kept an old amateur radio in a wooden cabinet for forty years. "Every voice you hear on this," he liked to say, "has travelled further than you think." Faris had never imagined that one day his own voice would be the one travelling upwards.

It all began with an announcement at school. Their science teacher, Mr Saleh, explained that the school had been selected for a live radio contact with the International Space Station. For roughly ten minutes, as the station passed overhead, students would be able to ask an astronaut questions directly. Because Faris had been helping his grandfather set up antennas for years, he was chosen to operate the radio during the contact. He spent the next three weeks practising call signs, checking cables and rehearsing questions until he could have recited them in his sleep.

The contact was scheduled for 8:42 p.m. on a Thursday, and by seven o'clock the school courtyard was packed with families. Parents sat in long rows of chairs, younger children waved small flags, and a local news team had set up a camera. Faris checked the antenna for the hundredth time, his stomach tight with nerves. His grandfather sat quietly near the back, his walking stick resting against his knee. Then, without warning, a hot wind rose from the desert, carrying a thick cloud of dust towards the school.

Within minutes, the dust storm had swallowed the lights of the town. Somewhere nearby a power line must have been damaged, because every lamp in the courtyard flickered and went out. The crowd fell silent, and then a hundred phone screens lit up in the darkness. Mr Saleh rushed over, his face pale. "The school generator won't start," he said. "Unless we find power in the next twenty minutes, we'll miss the station completely."

Faris felt as if weeks of preparation were about to be blown away by the wind. Then his grandfather placed a firm hand on his shoulder. "Don't lose hope so quickly," he said calmly, "because my old radio doesn't need the school's electricity — it runs perfectly well on a car battery." Faris stared at him in disbelief, pointing out that the radio was older than his own father. The old man simply smiled and replied, "Exactly, which is why it has survived far worse than a little dust."

What followed was a race against the clock. Faris's uncle drove the car as close to the courtyard as he could, while two older students carried the heavy wooden radio from the boot. With dust stinging their eyes, Faris and his grandfather connected the cables to the battery by torchlight. Luckily, the school's modern antenna was still standing, so they attached it to the old set. At 8:40, the radio crackled into life, hissing like a kettle about to boil.

At exactly 8:42, Faris pressed the button and spoke into the microphone, repeating the call sign he had practised so many times. For a few seconds there was only static, and he was sure they had failed. Then a calm voice cut through the noise: "This is the International Space Station. We hear you loud and clear." The courtyard exploded with cheers, and Faris had to wave his arms to make everyone quiet again. One after another, students stepped forward to ask about sleeping without gravity, growing plants in orbit, and what Earth looked like at night.

With less than a minute left, Faris asked the final question, which he had written himself. "What can you see right now?" After a short pause, the astronaut replied, "Actually, I can see a huge brown cloud stretching across northwest Arabia." He added with a laugh that someone down there was clearly having a very windy evening. Laughter swept through the dark courtyard, and then the voice faded into static as the station disappeared over the horizon.

Later that night, after the power had returned and the families had gone home, Faris sat on the roof with his grandfather once more. The storm had passed, and the sky had been washed clean, glittering with more stars than he could count. "You were right," Faris said. "Voices really do travel further than you think." His grandfather pointed to a small light moving steadily across the sky. "Yes," he said proudly, "and tonight, so did yours."

options: Faris's voice had travelled all the way into space

pages.text: Faisal Al-Harbi was famous at his school in Jeddah for one thing: his voice. As captain of the under-15 team, he could be heard from the car park, shouting instructions, warnings and encouragement at anyone who would listen. "Faisal doesn't need a whistle," Coach Nasser liked to joke. "He is the whistle." With the regional cup final only four days away, nobody could have predicted that this voice was about to disappear.

On Saturday morning, he woke up with a throat that felt as if it had been scraped with sandpaper. When he tried to say good morning to his mother, only a dry whisper came out. The doctor at the clinic examined him and shook her head. "It's laryngitis," she said. "If you want your voice back, you must rest it completely: no talking, and definitely no shouting, for at least a week." Faisal stared at her in horror, because the final was on Wednesday.

That evening he sat on the sofa feeling sorry for himself, typing angry messages on his phone. His younger cousin Hamad, who had been deaf since birth, was visiting with his parents. Hamad watched him for a while, then signed something to his father, who laughed. "He says you look like a lion that has lost its roar," his uncle translated. Faisal frowned, but then an idea struck him: if Hamad could say so much without a single sound, perhaps a captain could too.

The next day, Faisal turned up at training with Hamad and a notebook full of sketches. Coach Nasser was doubtful at first, but he agreed to give the plan a chance. Together, the cousins taught the team a set of simple hand signals: a closed fist meant "hold your position", two fingers pointing forward meant "press higher", and a flat hand moving down meant "slow the game". Some of the boys found it awkward and kept forgetting, while others treated it like a secret code from a spy film. By the end of the session, even Omar, the team's biggest sceptic, had to admit it was working.

Over the next two days, something unexpected happened. Because Faisal couldn't shout, everyone had to keep their heads up and look at one another constantly. The defenders began talking to each other more, and the midfielders started to anticipate each other's movements. "I used to wait for you to tell me what to do," admitted Ziyad, the shy left-back. "Now I actually have to think for myself." Faisal grinned and gave him a thumbs-up, which needed no translation.

On Wednesday afternoon, the stadium was packed with families, and the noise from the stands was deafening. Their opponents, Al-Noor Academy, were bigger and faster, and they had not lost a match all season. Within ten minutes, they had taken the lead with a powerful header from a corner. Faisal felt the old urge to scream at his team, but he swallowed it. Instead, he raised a calm, flat hand and lowered it slowly: slow down, stay together.

Gradually, his team regained control. Al-Noor's players communicated by shouting, but in the roar of the crowd, half their instructions were lost. Faisal's team, meanwhile, didn't need to hear anything; they only needed to look. Just before half-time, Faisal signalled with two fingers, and the whole team pressed high at once, catching Al-Noor's defenders off guard. Omar stole the ball and slotted it into the bottom corner to make it 1-1.

The second half was tense, and as the minutes ticked away, both teams were running on empty. Then, in the final minute, Faisal spotted a gap on the left wing. He couldn't call for Ziyad, so he simply caught his eye and pointed. Ziyad sprinted forward, received the pass and crossed the ball perfectly into the box. Faisal threw himself at it, and the ball flew past the goalkeeper into the net.

When the final whistle blew, his teammates lifted him onto their shoulders, cheering loudly enough for all of them. Up in the stands, Hamad was jumping up and down, signing something over and over. Faisal laughed and signed back the first phrase his cousin had ever taught him: "Thank you, brother." That evening, as he held the trophy, he realised that he had learned something more valuable than a victory. Sometimes the best leaders aren't the loudest people on the pitch; they're the ones who help everyone else find their own voice.

stories.title: The Star at the Edge of the World

pages.text: For three weeks, Yusuf had been giving Hamza the cold shoulder. They had been inseparable since primary school, sharing everything from football boots to exam nerves, so the silence felt heavier than any argument. It had all started with a video: a clip of Yusuf tripping over his own feet during a class presentation, slowed down and set to silly music. Within minutes, it had spread through the class group chat, and the account that posted it belonged to Hamza. When Hamza tried to explain, Yusuf simply walked away, too humiliated to listen.

So when Mr. Al-Harbi announced the pairs for the school hiking trip to Jebel Fihrayn, known as the Edge of the World, Yusuf's heart sank. "Yusuf and Hamza," the teacher read, without looking up from his clipboard. A few boys exchanged knowing glances. Yusuf considered asking for a change, but his pride wouldn't let him. "Fine," he muttered, though it was anything but fine.

The bus left Riyadh early in the morning, and by late afternoon the group was walking along the cliffs, where the land suddenly dropped hundreds of metres to the plain below. Hamza tried twice to start a conversation, but Yusuf kept his eyes fixed on the path. Determined to prove he didn't need anyone, Yusuf took a narrower trail to photograph an unusual rock formation, and Hamza, sighing, followed him. By the time they turned back, the rest of the class had disappeared over the ridge. The sun was sinking fast, and neither of their phones had a signal.

"We should have stayed with the group," Hamza said quietly. Yusuf opened his mouth to snap back, then bit his tongue, because Hamza was right. As they hurried down a rocky slope, Yusuf's foot slipped and he landed hard, gasping as pain shot through his ankle. Hamza was beside him in an instant, kneeling in the dust. "Don't move," he said. "Let me have a look."

Hamza had taken a first-aid course the previous summer, and he worked calmly, wrapping Yusuf's ankle tightly with a bandage from his backpack. Watching him, Yusuf felt a strange mixture of gratitude and guilt. "Why are you helping me?" he asked at last. "I've been horrible to you." Hamza tied the bandage and looked up. "Because you're my friend, even if you've forgotten it."

Darkness fell, and with it came a sharp desert chill. They had no idea which direction the camp lay in, but Yusuf, leaning against a boulder, noticed the stars appearing one by one. His grandfather had spent countless nights teaching him to find Al-Jadi, the North Star, just as travellers across the Arabian Peninsula had done for centuries. "The camp is north of the cliffs," he said, pointing upwards. "If we keep that star in front of us, we'll reach it." For the first time in weeks, Hamza smiled at him.

They moved slowly, Yusuf's arm over Hamza's shoulder, and somewhere along the way the silence between them finally broke. "About the video," Hamza began. "My cousin Majed was staying with us that weekend, and he borrowed my phone and posted it as a joke. I deleted it the moment I saw it, but by then everyone had already shared it." Yusuf stopped walking. "Why didn't you tell me?" "I tried," Hamza said simply. "You never let me finish a sentence."

Yusuf felt his face burn with shame. He had been so certain, so quick to judge, that he had never once considered that Hamza might be innocent. "I'm sorry," he said, and the words, which had seemed impossible for weeks, came out easily. "I should have trusted you. If I'd listened, we could have cleared the air ages ago." Hamza shrugged, grinning. "Well, you can make it up to me by never taking a shortcut again."

An hour later, they saw torches flickering ahead and heard Mr. Al-Harbi calling their names. The teacher's relief quickly turned into a long lecture about safety, which both boys accepted without complaint. Later, wrapped in blankets beside the fire, Yusuf found a weak signal on his phone and typed a message to the class group: "Hamza didn't post that video. He's the best friend anyone could ask for." Then he looked up at Al-Jadi, still shining steadily above them, and thought that some things, like stars and true friends, are easiest to find in the dark.

pages.text: Faris had always believed that almost any problem could be solved with a fully charged phone. So when his grandfather announced that he would take Faris and his cousin Yousef camping in the Nafud desert for three days, Faris downloaded four different map apps before they had even left Ha'il. "The desert doesn't care about your apps," Grandfather Saleh said with a smile as he loaded water containers into his old Land Cruiser. Faris laughed politely, but secretly he thought the old man was a little out of date.

For two days, the trip was everything Faris had hoped for. They cooked rice over a crackling fire, drank cardamom coffee, and followed the delicate tracks of a desert fox until they disappeared behind a dune. At night, Grandfather pointed out the stars, naming each one as though it were an old friend. "That one is Al-Jadi, the North Star," he explained. "Travellers in this land have trusted it for thousands of years." Yousef listened carefully, but Faris was too busy holding his phone in the air, hoping to catch enough signal to upload his photos.

On the third morning, they drove deeper into the sand to find a well that Grandfather remembered from his youth. Around noon, the sky turned a strange, sickly yellow, and the horizon began to blur. "Sandstorm," Grandfather said quietly, and he stopped the car at once. Within minutes, a wall of sand had swallowed the dunes, and the wind was howling like an angry animal. For hours they sat in the car with scarves over their faces, unable to see more than a metre beyond the windows.

By the time the storm had finally died down, it was late afternoon and the car was half-buried in sand. Worse still, the engine refused to start, no matter how many times Grandfather turned the key. Faris pulled out his phone and felt his stomach drop: there was no signal, the battery was at nine percent, and the map showed nothing but an empty grey screen. Grandfather, however, remained completely calm. "Your father's camp is about fifteen kilometres east," he said. "We'll walk once the sun goes down, because in this heat the sun would defeat us long before the distance did."

While they waited in the shade of the car, Grandfather taught them how to read the land. "The wind here usually blows from the same direction, so the dunes line up like waves on the sea," he explained, tracing their shape in the sand with his finger. "Learn their pattern, and they become a map." For the first time, Faris put his phone away and paid attention. Then, as they began climbing the first dune at sunset, Grandfather's foot slipped on the loose sand, and he fell with a sharp cry of pain.

His ankle was badly twisted, and he could only move slowly, leaning heavily on Yousef's shoulder. "Faris, you'll have to lead us," Grandfather said, his face tight with pain. Faris's heart sank, because without a screen to guide him he felt completely blind. Then, as the first stars appeared, he remembered the bright, steady light his grandfather had shown him. If the North Star was there, then east had to be on his right. He took a deep breath, lined himself up with the waves of sand, and stepped forward.

They walked for hours, stopping regularly so that Grandfather could rest his ankle. Every few minutes, Faris checked the star and the direction of the dunes, just to make sure they hadn't drifted off course. At one point, Yousef grabbed his arm and insisted that he could see lights far to the south. Faris hesitated, tempted to turn, but then he recalled his grandfather's warning that tired eyes often play tricks in the desert. "We keep going east," he said firmly, and Grandfather squeezed his shoulder. "Now," the old man whispered proudly, "you are reading the desert."

Just before dawn, Faris caught the faint smell of woodsmoke drifting across the sand. Moments later, a pair of headlights swept over the top of a dune, and a familiar voice called out their names. It was Faris's father, who had been searching with two friends ever since the storm had ended. He hugged all three of them so tightly that Yousef complained he couldn't breathe. "How on earth did you find your way?" his father asked, and Grandfather simply nodded towards Faris.

Back home in Ha'il, Faris plugged in his phone, but the first thing he did was buy a small notebook. On its first page, he carefully drew the North Star and the shape of the dunes, exactly as his grandfather had taught him. "So, will you delete all your map apps now?" Grandfather teased him. Faris grinned and shook his head. "No, but from now on I'll never trust them more than I trust the sky."

pages.text: Yousef had always believed that technology could solve any problem, including his grandfather. Grandpa Saleh still kept a paper diary, wound his watch every morning and wrote phone numbers on the back of his hand. So when his parents announced that the whole family would gather at Grandpa's house for Eid lunch, Yousef saw his chance. "This year," he told his younger sister Lama, "I'm going to drag Grandpa into the twenty-first century." Lama, who was eleven and far too wise for her age, simply raised an eyebrow.

Two days before Eid, Yousef arrived with a small grey speaker and a box of smart light bulbs. He spent the afternoon changing bulbs, climbing onto the roof to fix the internet cable and naming the assistant "Noor", because Grandpa liked the word. "You just talk to her," he explained proudly. "Say 'Noor, turn on the lights,' and she does it immediately." Grandpa leaned towards the speaker as if it were a nervous kitten and boomed, "NOOR, TURN ON THE LIGHTS!"

The lights stayed off. Instead, a calm voice replied, "Adding forty kilos of lemons to your shopping basket." Yousef grabbed his phone and cancelled the order, his ears turning bright red. "She's just getting used to your voice," he insisted. Grandpa nodded seriously and asked about the weather, but Noor set an alarm for four o'clock in the morning and announced that it would repeat every day "until further notice".

By the next morning, things had gone from bad to worse. The alarm had woken the entire street, and the neighbour's cat had been spotted on the roof, refusing to come down. When Grandpa asked Noor to call his brother Hamad, she played ten minutes of camel noises instead. Grandma, who had been preparing the kabsa since dawn, came out of the kitchen holding a wooden spoon. "Yousef," she said sweetly, which was always a bad sign, "if that machine speaks again before lunch, it will be sleeping in the garden."

Yousef was determined not to give up. He sat at the kitchen table for hours, adjusting settings, watching tutorials and muttering to himself. Lama brought him a cup of tea and watched with obvious enjoyment. "Have you considered," she said, "that maybe the problem isn't Grandpa?" Yousef didn't bother to reply, mainly because he was starting to wonder the same thing.

On Eid day, the house filled up with uncles, aunts, cousins and a mountain of dates. Everything was going smoothly until Uncle Majid, curious about the speaker, asked loudly, "Noor, what was Yousef's latest search?" Before Yousef could dive across the room, Noor answered clearly: "How to make Grandpa think I am a genius." There was a moment of silence, and then the whole room burst out laughing at once. Yousef wished the ground would open up and swallow him whole.

Just then, the doorbell rang. A delivery man stood outside, sweating, next to a tower of boxes. "Forty kilos of lemons for Mr Saleh," he announced. Yousef turned pale. "But I cancelled that order! I definitely cancelled it!" Behind him, Grandpa cleared his throat and calmly took out his own phone.

"You cancelled it," Grandpa said, his eyes twinkling, "so I ordered them again myself." He explained that he had been using a smartphone for three years, made video calls to his old friends in Jeddah and even paid his bills online. "While you were up on the roof fixing that cable, I connected Noor to my phone and changed a few settings," he admitted. "My grandson came to teach me, and I didn't have the heart to tell him I already knew. Besides, I wanted to see how far he would go." Across the room, Lama looked at Yousef and silently mouthed, "I told you."

The camel noises, it turned out, had been Grandpa's idea too, and he still thought they were hilarious. Yousef laughed until his stomach hurt, partly from relief and partly because he had been well and truly fooled. That afternoon, Grandma turned the lemons into jugs of fresh lemon and mint juice, and everyone agreed it was the best Eid drink they had ever tasted. Before leaving, Yousef hugged his grandfather and asked what he should teach him next year. "Next year," Grandpa replied with a grin, "I'll be teaching you."
